cards.title: The rule of thirds
cards.body: Imagine your frame split into a 3×3 grid. Place key subjects along the lines or at their intersections instead of dead center. Off-center instantly feels more dynamic and intentional.

cards.title: Leading lines pull the eye
cards.body: Roads, fences, rivers, shadows — any line that guides the viewer toward your subject adds depth and direction. Find a line in the scene, then put your subject where it ends.
A lone tree centered in the frame: fine, forgettable. The same tree on a third-line intersection, with a dirt road leading to it: suddenly it's a photograph. Nothing changed except placement.
Turn on your camera's grid overlay — every phone has it in settings. Compose with the grid for a week and the thirds become instinct. Then you can break the rule on purpose.

cards.q: Where should the subject go under the rule of thirds?
choices: Along the grid lines or intersections
cards.explain: The four intersection points are the power positions. Centering works for symmetry, but thirds create tension and balance.

flashcards.front: What is the rule of thirds?
flashcards.back: Divide the frame into a 3×3 grid; place subjects on the lines or intersections, not centered.
Lines in the scene — roads, rails, shores — that guide the viewer's eye toward the subject.
Empty areas around the subject that give it room to breathe and add drama.

flashcards.front: Why shoot from a different angle?
flashcards.back: Eye level is how everyone sees the world. Crouching low or climbing high makes ordinary subjects look extraordinary.

questions.q: Your horizon sits dead center and the shot feels flat. Fix?
choices: Move it to the upper or lower third
questions.explain: A centered horizon splits the image in two and kills energy. Give two-thirds of the frame to whichever half is more interesting.

questions.q: What's the fastest way to add depth?
choices: Include a foreground element or leading line
questions.explain: Layers — foreground, subject, background — create depth no gear can fake. A branch in the corner beats a new lens.

choices: It isolates the subject and adds mood
questions.explain: Emptiness is a compositional tool. A tiny subject in vast sky feels lonely; the same subject crammed edge-to-edge feels chaotic.

questions.q: A fence runs diagonally toward a barn. The fence is a…
questions.explain: Diagonal lines are the strongest guides — they pull the eye straight to wherever they converge.

questions.q: When is centering the subject the right call?
questions.explain: Rules serve the photo, not the reverse. Perfect symmetry — a reflection, a doorway — begs to be centered.

cards.title: Golden hour is cheat mode
cards.body: The hour after sunrise and before sunset gives warm, soft, directional light. Long shadows, glowing skin tones, dramatic skies — the same scene looks expensive, for free.

cards.title: Midday sun is harsh
cards.body: Overhead light at noon carves hard shadows and makes people squint. If you must shoot midday, find open shade — building shadows, big trees — for soft, even light.
Same portrait, two times of day. Noon: raccoon-eye shadows under the brows. 6pm golden hour: warm glow, soft shadows, catchlights in the eyes. The camera didn't change — the sun's angle did.
Backlight on purpose: put the sun behind your subject for a glowing rim around hair and shoulders. Tap your phone screen on their face so the camera exposes for them, not the sky.

cards.q: It's noon, harsh sun, no choice. Best move?
choices: Move the subject into open shade
Use the flash on full blast
cards.explain: Open shade turns the whole sky into a giant softbox — even, flattering light with no hard shadows.

flashcards.back: Roughly the first hour after sunrise and the last hour before sunset — warm, soft, low-angled light.

flashcards.front: Why avoid midday sun for portraits?
flashcards.back: Overhead light carves harsh shadows under eyes and noses, and makes people squint.
Light coming from behind the subject, creating a glowing rim — expose for the subject's face.
Diffused light with gentle shadow transitions — from shade, clouds, or large nearby surfaces.

questions.q: You want dreamy warm portraits. When do you shoot?
questions.explain: Low sun means warm color, soft shadows, and flattering direction. It's the most forgiving light that exists.

questions.q: Clouds roll in and the light goes flat and soft. This is…
choices: Only good for black and white
questions.explain: Overcast skies are nature's softbox. Colors get richer, shadows vanish — ideal for flowers, faces, and details.

questions.q: Your subject's face is dark against a bright sunset. Fix?
choices: Tap to expose for the face, or add fill light
Give up and shoot the sunset alone
questions.explain: Expose for what matters. Tapping the face tells the camera to prioritize it; a reflector or fill flash lifts the shadows.

questions.q: Side light is prized because it…
choices: Reveals texture and shape through shadows
questions.explain: Light raking across a surface shows every ripple and grain. Front light flattens; side light sculpts.

choices: The twilight after sunset with deep blue skies
The hour when flash is mandatory
questions.explain: Those 20–30 minutes after sunset: the sky goes cobalt, city lights pop on — prime time for skylines.

cards.title: The exposure triangle
cards.body: Three settings control brightness: aperture (the lens opening), shutter speed (how long it stays open), and ISO (sensor sensitivity). Change one and the others must compensate — it's a three-way seesaw.

cards.title: Aperture = depth of field
cards.body: Small f-number (f/1.8) means a wide opening and blurry backgrounds — perfect for portraits. Big f-number (f/11) means a narrow opening and everything sharp — what landscapes want. The numbers feel backwards until they click.
Portrait at f/1.8: the subject's eyes are razor sharp, the background melted into creamy blur. Same scene at f/11: the fence three meters back is sharp too. One dial, two completely different photos.
Shutter speed freezes or blurs motion: 1/500s freezes a runner, 1/30s turns a waterfall to silk. Rule of thumb: stay faster than 1/60s handheld, or your own shake blurs everything.

cards.q: You want a blurry background behind your subject. Which aperture?
cards.explain: Small f-number = wide aperture = shallow depth of field. f/1.8 melts backgrounds; f/11 and f/16 keep nearly everything sharp.

flashcards.front: What are the three exposure settings?
flashcards.back: Aperture (lens opening), shutter speed (time open), ISO (sensor sensitivity).

flashcards.front: What does a small f-number like f/1.8 do?
flashcards.back: Opens the aperture wide: more light, shallow depth of field, blurry backgrounds.
Fast ones — 1/500s or quicker. Slow speeds like 1/30s blur motion instead.
Grainy speckles that appear at high ISO. Raise ISO only when you need the brightness.

questions.q: Your landscape has a soft foreground and background. Fix?
choices: Use a smaller aperture like f/11
questions.explain: A narrow aperture (big f-number) deepens the sharp zone from near to far — exactly what landscapes want.

questions.q: Indoor photo too dark at f/2.8, 1/60s, ISO 400. Brighten without blur?
choices: Raise ISO and accept some noise
Slow the shutter to 1 second handheld
questions.explain: 1/60s is already the handheld floor and f/2.8 is wide open — ISO is the only dial left. Noise beats a black or blurry frame.

questions.q: What does ISO 3200 vs ISO 100 mean?
questions.explain: Each ISO doubling is one stop more sensitivity. 100 to 3200 is five stops (32x) — bright in the dark, grainy everywhere.

questions.q: You want silky waterfall blur. Settings?
questions.explain: Long exposures smear motion into silk — but any handshake smears everything too, so the tripod is non-negotiable.

questions.q: Aperture, shutter, and ISO are linked because…
choices: They all control exposure — change one, compensate with another
Cameras force you to use all three
They're the same setting with three names
questions.explain: It's a triangle: widen the aperture and you must quicken the shutter or drop ISO to hold the same brightness. Every exposure is a three-way trade.
